title: Inclusion Body Myositis
subject: Medicine
summary: A slowly progressive inflammatory muscle disease affecting adults over 50, characterised by quadriceps and wrist flexor weakness, rimmed vacuoles on biopsy, and poor response to steroids.

sections.p: Inclusion body myositis (IBM) is an idiopathic inflammatory myopathy that presents with insidious, asymmetric proximal and distal muscle weakness, predominantly in the quadriceps and wrist flexors. Diagnosis requires a combination of clinical features, elevated CK, EMG showing myopathic changes, and muscle biopsy demonstrating rimmed vacuoles and amyloid inclusions.

t.b: Is the patient’s creatine kinase elevated? A CK 2–5× upper limit of normal supports myopathy but is not specific.
Does the EMG show myopathic changes with fibrillation potentials? This indicates active muscle fibre damage.
Are rimmed vacuoles and amyloid inclusions present? Their presence confirms IBM and differentiates it from polymyositis.

sections.p: IBM is staged by the IBM Functional Rating Scale (IBMFRS), a 10‑item questionnaire scoring activities of daily living. Stage 1: mild weakness, stage 5: severe disability with wheelchair dependence.

t.b: What does a score of 7 indicate? Moderate functional impairment, likely needing assistive devices.

sections.p: The exact etiology is unknown; autoimmune mechanisms and viral triggers (e.g., CMV, EBV) are implicated. In low‑resource settings, chronic infections such as HIV and tuberculosis may coexist and worsen muscle damage.

t.b: Is the patient HIV positive? Coinfection can exacerbate muscle weakness and complicate treatment.

sections.p: Patients report insidious difficulty climbing stairs, rising from a chair, and lifting objects. Wrist flexor weakness leads to dropping items. Dysphagia may occur in advanced disease.

t.b: Which muscle groups are most affected? Quadriceps and wrist flexors show the greatest weakness.

sections.p: Baseline labs include CK, ESR, ANA, and HIV/TB screening. EMG and muscle biopsy are essential. Imaging (MRI) can show muscle oedema but is often unavailable.

t.b: Is ANA positive? Helps rule out systemic lupus.

sections.p: Rapid progression, respiratory muscle involvement, severe dysphagia, and weight loss warrant urgent review. Infection risk is higher due to immunosuppression.

t.b: Does FVC <50% predicted? Indicates respiratory muscle weakness.

sections.p: First treat any underlying infection. Supportive care includes physiotherapy, assistive devices, and nutritional support. Immunosuppressants (steroids, IVIG) have limited efficacy; consider trial of methotrexate or azathioprine if active inflammation is evident.

t.b: Why use methotrexate? It may reduce inflammation but monitor liver function.
Why avoid high-dose steroids? Risk of infection and poor response.

sections.p: Regular assessment with IBMFRS every 6 months. Monitor for dysphagia and respiratory compromise. Vaccinate against influenza and pneumococcus to reduce infection risk.

t.b: Does the patient choke on liquids? Early intervention prevents aspiration.

faq.q: Why do steroids not work well in IBM?
faq.a: IBM has a chronic, degenerative component with rimmed vacuoles; steroids mainly target inflammation and are ineffective against the degenerative process.

faq.q: Can I use IVIG for IBM?
faq.a: IVIG may provide short‑term benefit in selected patients but evidence is limited and it is costly.
No clear genetic link has been established; most cases are sporadic.

exam: What is the most characteristic muscle group affected in IBM? — Quadriceps and wrist flexors, leading to difficulty rising and dropping objects.
Which investigation is essential to confirm IBM? — Muscle biopsy showing rimmed vacuoles and amyloid inclusions.
A 55‑year‑old patient with progressive weakness and CK 300 IU/L is unresponsive to steroids. What is the next step? — Consider trial of methotrexate or azathioprine, monitor for infection.
How does IBM differ from polymyositis on biopsy? — IBM shows rimmed vacuoles; polymyositis shows end‑omarginal necrosis without vacuoles.
A patient presents with dysphagia and respiratory weakness. Which test should you order urgently? — Pulmonary function test (FVC) to assess respiratory muscle strength.
Which infection screening is mandatory before starting immunosuppression in a low‑resource setting? — HIV and TB screening.
Why is early physiotherapy important in IBM? — It helps maintain muscle strength and functional independence despite disease progression.
What is the significance of a normal CK in a patient with suspected IBM? — CK can be normal early; diagnosis relies on EMG and biopsy.
